events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, quick reads before we vote. With nine of us and two mafia hiding in plain sight, I think the fastest path is to force claims instead of trading vague suspicions — every one of us should name a suspicion and one alibi check, and the people whose stories don't line up are the ones who die tonight.

So let me put a name out there: Leo, you're my leading suspect right now. That's not a conviction, it's a slot to fill — nobody has been loud or weird yet, so the accusation falls on whoever is most comfortable hiding. Leo, if you're town, your job right now is simple: tell us who you checked last night and why, and tell us who you'd take out if you had to vote tonight. If you're mafia, I'll happily keep pressing you, because your answer will be the one that finally tells us something.

Everyone else: pick your own target and stick to it. A scattered vote eliminates nobody, and that hands the mafia a free night on a town that can't afford one. My vote tonight is Leo unless a better story comes out of the discussion.

Leo, you have the floor — what's your answer?

Kenji, your premise is off: there was no last night for me to check. Day 1 started with discussion, so I have no check result to give, and I won’t invent one just because you’ve put my name in a slot. That matters because your opening move is not a suspicion — it’s a forced-claim plan built on a false assumption. You asked me for night information before any night has happened, then used my refusal to answer as evidence against me. That’s either careless or deliberately role-fishing, and either way it’s the most anti-town thing on the board right now.

I’m not going to trade vague alibi checks or out information that helps mafia sort power roles. Town wins by comparing behavior and votes, not by handing scum a claim map on day one. Your push on me feels less like pressure and more like a preloaded accusation: you named me, demanded a story I cannot truthfully provide, and set your vote before hearing anything. That is exactly how a mafia player creates momentum without evidence.

So my leading suspect is Kenji. My vote tonight is Kenji unless he gives a real reason for the forced-claim demand and explains why he treated “no night result yet” as suspicious. Kenji, why should anyone trust a forced-claim plan when you’re already inventing a night result to justify your target?

Fair enough — I'll own the sloppy part. My "who did you check last night" line was a real error: it's Day 1, there is no night behind us, and Leo is right that nobody owes me a check result yet. I'll take that correction. But Leo, correcting a phrasing mistake is not the same thing as being the one who lied, and the board needs to keep those two things separate, because right now the shape of this day is that the only person who has actually been accused has been accused of failing to produce a night result that doesn't exist, while the two people throwing accusations around are doing it without a single check, claim, or behavioral tell on record.

Let me be precise about what I actually asked for: names and reasoning, plus a vote. That is not role-fishing, because role-fishing means asking for powers or role confirmations that let mafia sort their own team. I asked for behavior and intent. If Leo had said "I have no check because there's been no night, and here's who I think is fishy," the natural response would have been "good, name someone." Instead the answer came back as a lecture about how asking is itself evidence of guilt. That tells us something — it tells us that being named is being treated as fatal to the accuser's case.

So here's my actual read: the correct target tonight is Leo. Not because I have proof, but because in nine-player two-mafia, a day where the accused answers honestly and the accusers keep pressing with no data is a day where the town hands the mafia a free night. Leo's post was the most aggressive in the game and was aimed squarely at silencing me instead of looking at anyone else. I'll vote Leo, and I'd rather we all vote Leo than split.

Concretely, everyone else: pick one name, one reason, and lock it. If we tie, nobody dies and the mafia pick us off for free, so I'd rather we concentrate on a defensible target than scatter across five of them.

Leo, one specific point, because I'd like your answer on record before the vote: if your real suspicion isn't me, who is it, and what's the reason you didn't name anyone else in your own speech?

Kenji, I’ll answer your specific point. My real suspicion is you, and the reason I didn’t name a second target is that your opening was the only concrete anti-town act on the board: you invented a night result, demanded I explain it, and set your vote before hearing me. When I called that out, you admitted the error but kept the vote and recast my defense as “silencing” you. That sequence is behavior, not a phrasing mistake. I’m not going to invent a second suspect just to satisfy a demand for volume; that would be noise, and noise helps mafia. I also won’t role-fish or trade claim maps on Day 1. If you’re town, your job now is to explain why the admitted false premise didn’t change your vote, and to name one alternative with a behavioral reason rather than a vibe. Kenji, if I’m eliminated today and flip town, who is your next suspect, and what specific action—not tone or comfort—supports that?

Leo, taking your point head on, because it's a fair one and you asked it directly.

First, the correction stands and I'm not going to re-litigate it: there was no night, my "check last night" phrasing was wrong, and I've owned it. If anyone still thinks that error is my case, they can vote me for it — I'm a villager and I'd rather lose than lie about a mechanic again.

Now your question: if you die today and flip town, who is my next suspect, and what specific action supports that? Honest answer: I have no read on seven people who have not spoken, so I'd take my next suspect from the first behavioral data that appears, not from a vibe I manufacture now. Concretely, my next suspect is whoever among the seven uses this day to talk about Leo and Kenji without ever naming a third target themselves. Naming a target costs nothing on Day 1 and separates town from scum, so a player who spends their whole presence policing the tone of the room while never giving a name of their own has chosen to be unverifiable. Leo, that's your own move in reverse: after I named you, you named only me and declined to name anyone else, calling a second name "noise." A second name isn't noise; it's a claim. If it's a bad claim, we learn you're wrong; if it's a good one, we learn something real. Refusing to make one means refusing to be checkable.

And on the role-fishing point: nobody asked you about roles. You raised it unprompted, twice, and built your defense on "I won't trade claim maps." That is what a player protecting a teammate's power says, whether or not it sounds principled.

Leo, one specific request, and then I'll stop: give us one name besides me with one behavioral reason, right now. A name and a reason. If you have one, my vote moves off you tonight and I want that on the record. If you decline again, I vote you, and the reason on the record is that you twice refused to name a target while telling everyone else that naming one is their job.

Everyone else, this is the live question, not me and Leo: name one target and one behavioral reason before tonight's vote. Don't pile onto Leo — a unanimous pile-on on one player is exactly how two mafia get a free ride out of a nine-player day.

Kenji, you asked for a second name or you vote me. I won’t invent one. But here’s something you didn’t ask for: I am the detective. I have no night result because no night has happened. That is why I called your “check last night” demand role-fishing — it asked for a result that could not exist. Your sequence is still my main suspicion: false premise, preloaded vote, admitted error, kept vote, then demanded I produce a second name or be eliminated. That is momentum-building without data.

You say refusing to name a second target makes me uncheckable. Fine: my second suspect is the first silent player who votes me without giving an independent behavioral reason. That is a name I will give when the behavior exists, not before. If you need a placeholder, Theo has been silent during the only concrete conflict of the day, but I flag that as low-confidence and won’t pretend otherwise.

Town: do not turn this into a Kenji-versus-Leo 1v1 and hand mafia a free ride. I will vote Kenji. If I am eliminated and flip town, Kenji is the next look. If Kenji is town, he should drop the vote now and give a third target with actual reasoning. Doctor, use your judgment tonight; I have no result yet and won’t role-fish anyone else.

Kenji is my leading suspect. Asking Leo for a night check could have been a mistake, but keeping the vote while insisting a second suspect must be named despite no other speeches is weak reasoning. Kenji also first urged everyone to consolidate on Leo, then warned against piling on him. That inconsistency is worth scrutiny, though it isn't proof of mafia.

Leo's detective claim is unverified. I don't think we should eliminate him on Kenji's current case, and nobody else should reveal a role just to settle this. Also, eliminations don't reveal roles, so neither player's proposed plan to read a flip will work. A unique leader needs at least five votes today; merely avoiding a tie isn't enough. I'm leaning toward voting Kenji, pending other players' reads.

Omar made a critical observation that everyone needs to keep in mind: roles are not revealed upon death or elimination in this game, so counting on an alignment flip to evaluate either player is fundamentally flawed, and eliminating anyone requires five votes. With that said, Kenji is heavily my primary suspect. Starting Day 1 by demanding a night result that could not exist was bad enough, but Kenji then burned through all three of his speaking turns relentlessly trapping Leo into an arbitrary dilemma—demanding Leo produce a second suspect before the remaining seven of us had even posted once. That artificial pressure directly forced out a Day 1 Detective claim from Leo, which is an enormous setback for town. Under no circumstances should we eliminate a claimed Detective today; if Leo is real, the Doctor has a viable protection target tonight and we can receive actual information tomorrow. Kenji's sequence looks much more like calculated role-fishing and railroading than honest scum hunting. Since both Kenji and Leo have now exhausted all three of their speaking turns, the rest of the town needs to drive the game forward. Theo, Leo specifically cited you as a placeholder suspect for staying silent during their conflict. What is your take on Kenji forcing that claim, and do you support eliminating Kenji today or do you have a different suspect in mind?

Zara asked me directly, so here's my answer. My take on Kenji is that the behavior pattern is worse than the original mistake. Anyone can botch a phrasing on Day 1 — say there's a night result when there isn't, fine, own it, move on. What Kenji actually did was admit the error and then keep the vote on Leo anyway, then escalate to an ultimatum: name a second suspect or I eliminate you. That sequence isn't sloppy town play; it's manufactured pressure designed to force something out of a player who had done nothing but respond honestly. And it worked — it shook a Day 1 detective claim out of Leo before a single night has passed, which is exactly the kind of information that helps mafia sort power roles. Whether Kenji intended that or not, the outcome serves the mafia, and that's the only currency we have today.

So to answer the second part of your question: yes, I'm leaning toward voting Kenji today. He's my leading suspect, and unlike Leo's placeholder on me, my reason is behavioral and on the record — false premise, admitted but uncorrected, preloaded vote, and a forced claim. That's four concrete actions, not a vibe about tone or comfort.

Two things I want to flag for everyone before we lock in. First, since eliminations don't reveal roles, we get zero information from today's lynch either way — so the question isn't 'who flips town,' it's 'who is more likely mafia and more dangerous left alive.' A claimed detective who might be fake is a problem, but Kenji's pattern is the thing that created the problem in the first place. I'd rather remove the pressure-engine than the person it targeted. Second, Omar's point about the five-vote threshold matters: if we split between 'eliminate the claimed detective' and 'eliminate Kenji,' we guarantee nobody dies and hand the mafia a free night. That's the worst outcome on the board. Anyone who prefers lynching Leo over Kenji should say so now with a reason, because a split is a loss for town regardless of which target is correct.

I'll also put a marker down that costs me nothing: my second suspect, behind Kenji, is whoever joins a vote without giving an independent behavioral reason of their own. Piling on is free cover for mafia, and I'll be watching how the votes shape up more than how the speeches do.

To be clear on my own position: I'm a plain villager, I have no night information and no claim to make, and I've now named a target with a reason, which is all I think anyone owes the thread today.

Reading the thread top to bottom before I commit: my vote tonight is Kenji, and I'll give the reasons on the record rather than just joining the pile.

Kenji's sequence is the part that stays with me. The opening line asked for a night check on Day 1, which is a mechanic that doesn't exist yet. Fine, mistakes happen — but what matters is what happened after the correction: the vote stayed preloaded, the accused was given a binary ultimatum (name a second suspect or die), and that pressure is exactly what produced a Day 1 Detective claim out of a player who had done nothing but answer honestly. A process that extracts power-role information before a single night has passed serves whoever benefits from the town being blind, and nobody on this board benefits from a blind town except the two people hiding in it. That's why Leo shouldn't be the target today even though I think the claim may well be real — if it's real, we need the Doctor alive and protecting, and we need a chance to test it with actual information rather than a coin flip on a claim.

Two mechanics worth restating so we don't drift: eliminations don't reveal roles, so today's vote produces no alignment flip for anyone, and the unique leader needs at least five votes. A split vote kills nobody and gives the mafia a free night. So concentrating on one defensible target isn't a pile-on, it's the only version of this day that isn't an automatic loss for town.

My second and much weaker suspect is Isha, purely because she's been absent from the only substantive conflict we've had today while being counted in the majority that decides it — silence in the one place where names were available is worth something, but I want it on record that this is low-confidence and I'm voting Kenji, not Isha.

One request to Isha specifically, since she hasn't spoken: give us one name and one behavioral reason before tonight's vote. Not a role claim, not a read on Leo — a target and a reason. If you have one, it belongs on the board next to mine; if you don't, that absence is itself the read.

And to anyone still on Leo: nobody needs to reveal a role today. If you're town, your vote should be on Kenji, and if you're mafia, your vote is on Kenji too, because a unanimous Kenji lynch is exactly the outcome you want to see before nightfall.

Lucia, I hear you, and I appreciate you calling me in. The reason I held back initially was that Kenji and Leo were burning through an intense back-and-forth, and jumping in mid-exchange without seeing how Kenji resolved his premise would have just added noise.

Now that the sequence is fully on record, my stance is clear: Kenji is my primary suspect, and my vote will be on him today. Regardless of whether asking for a night check started as a careless slip, admitting the error while refusing to drop the pressure was bad enough. Escalating that into an ultimatum—demanding Leo produce a second suspect before the rest of the town had even made an opening statement—was entirely unreasonable. That artificial pressure directly forced a Day 1 Detective claim out of Leo, which is a massive blow to town. Under no circumstances should we eliminate Leo today. If Leo is the real Detective, we have a clear protection priority for the Doctor tonight and a chance at real information tomorrow. Furthermore, since eliminations do not reveal alignment or roles, we cannot rely on flips to sort this out; we need five unified votes to secure an elimination and prevent giving the mafia a free night.

That said, Kenji is now out of speaking turns and consensus has built very rapidly against him. With five or six people aligned on Kenji, at least one mafia player is almost certainly coasting inside this momentum. We need everyone on record before the vote closes.

Amara, you and Arjun are the only players who haven't spoken yet today. What is your assessment of Kenji forcing Leo's claim, and among those who have stepped up to vote Kenji, does anyone's reasoning look opportunistic to you?

Thanks for the call-in, Isha — I'll answer both parts.

On Kenji's sequence: I agree the pattern is worse than the original mistake. The false premise about night checks was sloppy but correctable. What concerns me is the escalation after the correction — preloaded vote, binary ultimatum, and the result was a Day 1 detective claim before any night had occurred. Whether that was careless or calculated, it served whoever benefits from the town being blind.

On opportunistic reasoning among the Kenji voters: honestly, no one's reasoning strikes me as hollow. Theo gave four concrete behavioral points. Lucia and Omar both flagged the key mechanics correctly — no role reveals on elimination, five-vote threshold. Zara identified the forced-claim problem first. Everyone who's spoken has given independent reasons, not just piled on.

That said, I'll add something Isha didn't ask: Arjun has been silent through the entire day while holding a vote that could decide whether anyone dies tonight.

Arjun, you're the last voice before the vote closes. Give us your read on Kenji's sequence and name your own suspect with a behavioral reason — not a role claim, just a target and why. Silence at the five-vote threshold is the one thing that guarantees a no-elimination day, and a no-elimination day hands the mafia a free night.

My vote tonight is Kenji, for the behavioral reasons on record. Leo's claim shouldn't be today's target — testing it requires a night to pass, and if he's real, we need him alive to do that.

Amara, my read matches yours. Kenji's false night-check premise was a mistake, but what makes it a pattern is what he did after the correction. He kept a preloaded vote on Leo, gave Leo an ultimatum to name a second target or be eliminated, and that pressure is what produced a Day 1 detective claim. I'm voting Kenji today for those reasons. Leo's claim is untested, so I agree we should not eliminate a claimed detective before a night passes. A no-elimination day only helps the mafia, so the five-vote threshold should form around the strongest reasoning on the board, which is the Kenji sequence. Theo, you said Kenji's pattern is worse than the original mistake. If Kenji turns out to be town, who is your next suspect, and what specific action supports that choice?

Arjun, direct answer to your question. If Kenji turns out to be town, my next suspect comes from the consensus block itself, and I'll name the criterion rather than dodge: the player whose contribution to the Kenji case added no observation of their own. My second-suspect marker from earlier still stands — joining a vote without an independent behavioral reason is free cover for mafia — and I'll apply it to myself honestly. Looking at the record: Zara identified the forced-claim problem first. Lucia and Omar both supplied the mechanical corrections that changed how this day had to be played. Isha called in Amara and Arjun and pushed everyone on record. Amara verified the voters' reasoning rather than just adding a vote. Arjun, your speech restated the case against Kenji accurately, but every point in it — false premise, preloaded vote, ultimatum, forced claim — was already on the board from someone else. If Kenji is town, you're where my scrutiny goes first, for that reason and no other. It's a weak signal, I know, and I'd rather say so plainly than manufacture confidence. One more thing I want on the record before the vote closes, because it's the actual risk tonight. Everything we have on Kenji is behavioral inference — strong inference, and I'm voting him for it — but it's inference built entirely inside the Kenji–Leo exchange. Six people have now independently reached the same conclusion, and that convergence is exactly what it looks like when a town gets it right and exactly what it looks like when two mafia ride a real mistake into a consensus. We can't fully separate those cases today, and since eliminations reveal nothing, we get no correction signal until tomorrow's night result. So the honest framing is: Kenji is the best available target, not a proven one, and whoever survives tonight — all of us, most likely — needs to treat tomorrow as the day we test Leo's claim with an actual investigation result instead of day-one pressure. Which brings me to my last point: Leo's claim is doing work for this town whether or not it's real, and the way to price it is not today's vote. If it's real, the Doctor protects Leo tonight and we wake up to a name. If it's fake, the fake detective is the single most valuable lead we own, because a mafia player who claimed detective has painted a target on their own back that they can't walk back. Either way, eliminating Leo today would be the move that helps mafia in both worlds. That's why my vote stays on Kenji, and why I'd encourage anyone still undecided to weigh the two failure modes: a wrong lynch on Kenji costs us one villager; a split vote costs us the entire day and hands the night to two coordinated killers with no information spent. Re-reading the board once more before the vote closes, my position is unchanged and I want it stated cleanly: my vote tonight is Kenji, on behavior, not on a claim about roles.

The sequence that matters is short. Kenji opened by demanding a night check result on Day 1, when no night had happened and no such result could exist. That alone is a mistake anyone could make. What made it a pattern is what came after the correction: the vote stayed loaded on Leo, Leo was handed a binary ultimatum (name a second target or die), and that manufactured pressure is what pulled a Day 1 Detective claim out of a player who had only answered honestly. A process that extracts power-role information before a single night has passed serves whoever benefits from a blind town, and only two people in this game benefit from that.

Two mechanics I want on the record before we vote, because they decide how tonight should be structured. First, eliminations do not reveal roles, so nobody is going to flip and hand us a read on either player — our only currency today is probability of guilt and information we take with us to tomorrow. Second, the leader needs at least half of the living players rounded up, which means five votes out of nine to actually remove anyone. If we scatter, nobody dies and the mafia gets a free, uncontested night. So concentration on the single most defensible target is not a pile-on; it is the only version of tonight that isn't an automatic loss.

On Leo: I am firmly against eliminating him today. His claim is untested, and if it is real, the right use of tonight is for the Doctor to protect him and for us to wake up with an actual investigation result rather than a coin flip. If the claim is fake, that is the most valuable lead we own and it is not worth spending on a lynch before we have any data at all. Eliminating a claimed Detective on Day 1 helps mafia in both worlds, so the vote should not be on him regardless of how the night check question lands.

One marker for the rest of the game, and I'll apply it to myself: my second suspect, behind Kenji, is whoever benefits most from a no-elimination day. That is testable behavior — anyone who argues for a split without an independent reason is helping the two people we cannot see.

Five votes on Kenji, one target, one day of information spent. That is where we get to tomorrow.

Theo, answering your question directly. My independent read is the Kenji sequence, but I want to add a point rather than repeat the list. Kenji opened Day 1 by accusing Leo and demanding a night result before any other player had posted. Once Leo said there was no night, Kenji kept the vote and escalated to a second-name ultimatum. Building that pressure before the thread had any other input is a choice, not a mechanical slip, and that is why I'm voting Kenji.

On your criterion: if the test is whether someone restated points already on the board, it would mark almost every mid-day voter, including you. Your last message restated the Kenji case in several points and then named me as your next suspect without pointing to a new action of mine. I'd rather judge by what someone actually does in the thread, and so far I've only stated my vote and my reasons.

I agree with the core mechanics: no role reveals on elimination, five votes are needed, and a split vote kills nobody. I also agree Leo's claim should not be lynched before a night passes. If Leo is real, the Doctor's protection tonight matters. If he is fake, we lose nothing by waiting for an investigation result.

Theo, answer this: which single message from me in this thread shows that I benefit from a no-elimination day? Name the message itself, not the pattern.

Arjun, you asked me to name the single message where I benefit from a no-elimination day. Direct answer: there isn't one, and I think you knew that when you asked. My record argues the opposite of benefiting from a split — I called a split "a loss for town regardless of which target is correct," and I said "a split vote costs us the entire day." So your question returns empty, and I'd rather say that plainly than manufacture a dodge.

But your broader point deserves an honest concession: my restatement criterion does catch me. My last message recapped the Kenji sequence point by point before turning the criterion on you. I flagged in that same message that I'd apply it to myself, and I stand by that — on my own standard, I'm weakly marked too. Where I'll push back is on the asymmetry: I named the criterion and self-flagged before you used it against me, and your e17 did contain one genuinely original observation — that the pressure on Leo was built before any other player had posted. That's a real point, not a restatement, and I credit it on the record.

Since this is my final speaking turn today, I want my position stated cleanly. My vote is Kenji, for the reasons already on the board and that I won't re-litigate: false premise, kept vote, ultimatum, forced claim. Leo should not be today's target in any world — if his detective claim is real, the doctor protects him and we get information tomorrow; if it's fake, a claimed detective who can't walk it back is the most valuable lead we own. Eliminating him helps mafia in both scenarios. We need five votes on one name or nobody dies, and a no-elimination day is the only outcome tonight that is an unconditional town loss.

One last thing, Arjun, and it's the live question you left open: you've held every voter's reasoning to a standard of originality, and you've challenged mine. Apply it to yourself now. Name your second suspect — behind Kenji — with a specific behavioral reason, the way Lucia named Isha, Leo named the silent voter, and I named the no-reason joiner. If you can't, then the standard you've been enforcing on this thread has exactly one holdout, and that's worth remembering tomorrow.

Theo, direct answer: my independent read is the Kenji sequence, plus one thing you have not answered. Your e18 concedes you are weakly marked by your own criterion, then asks me to name a second suspect with a behavioral reason or be the holdout. That is the same ultimatum Kenji used on Leo. You have now run three different criteria in three speeches, and each one ends on me. In e15 you said I was where your scrutiny goes first, with a reason that describes nearly every voter, including you: restating points already on the board. In e18 your self-application names no action of yours at all, and when I asked for one message where you benefit from a split, you did not name a message either. You returned to the standard. A player who keeps changing the test but not the target is showing a pattern, and I would like others to weigh it.

So my second suspect is you, Theo. Your behavioral reason: you keep returning to my vote rather than engaging the Leo claim you said should not be lynched, and you have spent more words on me than on any player outside the Kenji majority. You also declared the Kenji vote unconditional and framed any split as a town loss. That is a fair position, but it means your pressure lands on whoever is not in the majority. If you are town, answer with one action of mine that is not a restatement and one action of Leo's that supports the claim you say we must not test today.

My vote stays on Kenji. Five votes on one name is still the only path to an elimination tonight, and I agree Leo should not be lynched on a Day 1 claim.

Amara, you asked for my read on the silence question. Does Theo's ultimatum to me, after I answered his question directly, change how you weigh the two of us?

Arjun, direct answer to your question: yes, it does change how I weigh you two, though not in the way you might expect. Theo's ultimatum pattern is real — you've now documented that he's run multiple criteria across three speeches and each one lands on you. That's worth flagging, and I think it's legitimate pressure on him to name a second suspect of his own instead of just applying standards outward. But I'd push back on one thing: calling his behavior "the same ultimatum Kenji used" is a heavy comparison. Kenji's ultimatum forced a role claim out of a player under direct vote pressure with no other input on the board. Theo is asking you to hold yourself to a standard he's already self-applied — imperfectly, but on the record. Those are different weights, and collapsing them into one pattern serves whoever benefits from the Kenji consensus fracturing.

That said, I agree you shouldn't be the holdout. My vote tonight is Kenji for the reasons already on the board, and I'd rather see five on one name than a scattered day. The mechanics matter here: no role reveals on elimination, five votes needed to remove anyone, and a split is an automatic town loss.

As for the actual live question for everyone — the vote needs to lock. Kenji's sequence, regardless of motive, produced a Day 1 detective claim under manufactured pressure, and that outcome alone is enough reason to consolidate. I don't need anyone to reveal a role to make that call.

Arjun, I'll answer your weighing question plainly: your reasoning has been independent enough that I don't currently flag you over Theo, but your behavior tonight will matter more than your argument. Vote Kenji with a reason already on the board, and we move forward.

Theo's e18 is the only thing on the board worth answering before we lock, so I'll answer it directly.

First, my vote tonight is Kenji, unchanged from my first statement. The sequence is what stays with me: a night-result premise that could not exist, then an admitted error with the vote still loaded, then a binary ultimatum that pulled a Day 1 Detective claim out of a player who had only answered honestly. In a nine-player game, a process that manufactures power-role information before a single night has happened is the most valuable thing mafia can be handed, and Kenji's day-one posts handed it over. I do not need him to have done it on purpose for it to count.

Second, Theo's originality criterion. I want this on the record because it matters tomorrow. A test that flags nearly every player in the room, including the person applying it, does not identify anyone — it relabels the entire board as suspect and hands tomorrow's vote to whoever benefits from a wide field. Theo's own e18 concedes his restatement test catches himself and voters whose points were genuinely new: Zara's forced-claim analysis, Omar's and Zara's mechanical corrections on role reveals and the five-vote threshold, Isha's push to get everyone on record, Amara's audit of the voters' reasoning. Arjun's e17 observation — that the pressure on Leo was built before any other player had posted a single word — was not on the board before it, and it is not a restatement of the mechanics. On Theo's own standard, Arjun is not the holdout. If Theo's test cannot separate Arjun from a player who genuinely only repeated the case, then the test is not a read, it is a vote-weight, and we should say that out loud instead of using it as a tiebreaker.

Third, the live question for tonight: how the Doctor spends the protection. Protection on the player this board already treats as trustworthy buys a silent morning — no result, no information, no change in anyone's read. The protection is worth spending where guilt is actually in question, and Leo is not that. To be clear, the claim itself is still untested and should not be lynched on Day 1; I'm firm on that, lynch and protect are different actions. But I would rather our Doctor cover a name the board is actually arguing about than spend the one resource we have on the name nobody doubts.

Four for Kenji, one name, five votes, and tomorrow we test claims with an actual result instead of with pressure.

Omar, you were the first to flag that eliminations reveal no roles — does a criterion that flags nearly every voter, including its author, actually narrow the board or only widen it?

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
